items.why: Directly contrasts the five spies who enter with those who remain at the gate.
The sequence supports the key, but the priest also takes the same items moments later.
The thornbush is explicitly asked to rule the trees, while the competitor borrows unrelated wording.
The passage directly attributes prosperity to the land lacking nothing.
The stated reason is explicit, and the no-king detail is a plausible nearby distractor.
Jotham’s fear of his brother Abimelek is stated directly.
The passage clearly distinguishes the relatives carrying the message from its audience.
His purpose is explicitly to find somewhere else to stay, not specifically Micah’s house.
The requested mutual joy immediately precedes the conditional fire curse, though the phrasing is somewhat awkward.
The referent is recoverable, but 'does something' is vague and tests pronoun tracking more than content.
The report concerns people going to the fields, though the later sighting of them leaving the city is closely related.
The mother names her son, but the subsequent narration says a silversmith actually makes the idol.
The servant clearly kills Abimelek, although the key is phrased as an outcome rather than a person.
The occupants explicitly die when the stronghold is set on fire.
The priesthood’s endpoint is explicitly captivity, distinct from the idol’s use during Shiloh’s period.
The shouting immediately prompts the turn, but being overtaken occurs just beforehand and may also seem causal.
The fig tree’s rhetorical answer identifies giving up its sweet fruit as the reason.
The doorway approach has the specific purpose of setting the tower on fire, beyond the broader attack.
The command explicitly says to go and take over the land.
Micah directly states that the Levite becoming his priest grounds his expectation.
The route explicitly places the hill country immediately before Micah’s house, despite awkward question wording.
Jerub-Baal is the intended antecedent, but the shifts among Abimelek, family, and father complicate the pronoun.
Zebul is explicitly the covert sender, while Gaal is the person being reported.
They address the priest to inquire of God, cleanly separating intermediary from source.
The curse is presented as part of the punishment, so saying it happens after punishment is imprecise.
Zebul explicitly reinterprets the alleged people as mountain shadows.
Jotham directly gives God listening to them as the intended result.
The olive tree explicitly cites giving up its honoring oil as the reason for refusal.
Micah explicitly says his mother uttered the curse.
The cursing occurs while they eat and drink at the festival, clearly after grape work.
The lack of rescue is directly explained by distance from Sidon and absence of other ties.
